article.title: Why Correlation Can Disappear After Segmentation

paragraphs.en: An overall association can become weaker, disappear, or even reverse after data is divided into meaningful groups. Suppose a retailer finds that customers using a premium channel spend more than customers using a standard channel. It is tempting to conclude that the premium channel causes higher spending. But premium users may also be older, wealthier, or longer-tenured. Within each tenure group, the spending difference might be much smaller. Segmentation reveals that part of the overall correlation came from a different mix of customers. This is related to confounding and, in extreme cases, Simpson’s paradox. The key lesson is that aggregate relationships combine within-group relationships and differences in group composition. Analysts should choose segments based on the data-generating process rather than search randomly until a preferred result appears. Pre-treatment characteristics such as region, customer age, tenure, or historical value can be useful when they plausibly influence both exposure and outcome. Post-treatment variables require more caution because conditioning on them can create bias. Statistical adjustment through regression, stratification, matching, or weighting can help describe conditional relationships, but causal claims still require assumptions. Visualization is valuable: show the overall relationship and then the same relationship within important groups. If the pattern changes, explain why the composition matters. A disappearing correlation is not a failed analysis. It can be evidence that the original aggregate metric mixed different populations. Strong analytical communication distinguishes the observed association from the mechanism proposed to explain it. Analysts should define the population, timing, comparison, and uncertainty before turning an observed pattern into a business conclusion.
